result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.eulerize()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Make the graph Eulerian by duplicating as few edges as possible. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L38884-L38987){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.eulerize(weighted=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Eulerize](/assets/graphs/eulerize.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a square with a roof; badges give each node's degree, and only the top corners B and C are odd (accent color). Right: eulerize() returns a new graph with the edge B-C duplicated (accent arc), the cheapest fix, so every degree is even and the graph has an Eulerian circuit." width="100%"} A graph has an Eulerian circuit only if every node has even degree. `eulerize()` fixes the odd-degree nodes by pairing them up and duplicating the edges along a shortest path between each pair, choosing the pairing that adds the least in total. This is the construction behind the *Chinese postman problem*: the shortest closed route that traverses every street at least once is an Eulerian circuit of the eulerized graph, and the duplicated edges are the streets walked twice. Path lengths count hops, or total edge weight on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`), unless `weighted=` says otherwise; with weights, the added edges have the smallest total weight. The pairing is exact for up to 20 odd-degree nodes and a close approximation (greedy pairing improved by local swaps) beyond that. The result is a new graph with the same nodes (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and edges, plus the duplicates. Each duplicate copies its original edge's weight and attributes and is marked with the edge attribute `eulerize_added = True`; the original edges get `eulerize_added = False`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to measure path lengths by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph that is Eulerian (`is_eulerian()` returns `True`). The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or not connected (isolated nodes are ignored), or weights are used and one is negative. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path of four nodes has odd ends; duplicating its three edges makes a there-and-back circuit: ::: {#581ac75d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(4) walk = path.eulerize() walk.count_edges(), walk.is_eulerian(), walk.eulerian_circuit() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (6, True, [3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3]) ``` ::: ::: The duplicates are marked, so the extra distance of the postman route is easy to read. In a square with a roof, only the top corners have odd degree, so the edge between them is walked twice: ::: {#41a7372e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} house = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["bl", "br", "tl", "tr", "roof"]) .add_edges([("bl", "br"), ("bl", "tl"), ("br", "tr"), ("tl", "tr"), ("tl", "roof"), ("tr", "roof")]) ) walk = house.eulerize() added = walk.get_edge_df().filter(eulerize_added=True) label = walk.get_label_from_id [(label(s), label(t)) for s, t in added.select(["source", "target"]).iter_rows()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('tl', 'tr')] ``` ::: :::
